notes_list.title: Acidity of Organic Compounds & Conjugate Base Stability
notes_list.basic_overview: The acidity of an organic molecule ($HA \rightleftharpoons H^+ + A^-$) is directly determined by the thermodynamic stability of its conjugate base anion ($A^-$). A lower $pKa$ value signifies a stronger acid. Conjugate base stabilization is governed by six key electronic factors: Atom Electronegativity/Size, Resonance Delocalization, Inductive Effects ($-I$), Hybridization (s-character), Aromatic Stabilization, and Steric/Solvation dynamics.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The Ortho Effect in benzoic acids: Any ortho-substituent (regardless of $+I/-I$ or $+M/-M$, except steric exceptions like tiny groups) increases acidity relative to meta/para isomers by forcing the carboxyl group out of ring coplanarity (relieving steric strain) and preventing cross-conjugation with the ring. Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) has $pKa \approx 0.38$, comparable to mineral acids, due to extensive $-M$ resonance stabilization of the phenoxide charge.
notes_list.examples: 1. Mineral vs Organic Acids: Picric acid ($pKa = 0.38$) > Acetic acid ($pKa = 4.76$) > Phenol ($pKa = 9.95$) > Ethanol ($pKa = 16$). 2. Hybridization: Terminal alkynes ($HC\equiv CH, sp, pKa = 25$) > Ethylene ($H_2C=CH_2, sp^2, pKa = 44$) > Ethane ($H_3C-CH_3, sp^3, pKa = 50$). 3. Inductive dependence: $FCH_2COOH (pKa=2.59) > ClCH_2COOH (pKa=2.87) > BrCH_2COOH (pKa=2.90) > ICH_2COOH (pKa=3.18)$. 4. Aromaticity driving acidity: Cyclopentadiene ($pKa = 15$) is unusually acidic because losing a proton yields the 6$\pi$ aromatic cyclopentadienyl anion.
notes_list.conditions_and_medium: Polar protic solvents (e.g., $H_2O$, $MeOH$) stabilize small, localized anions through strong hydrogen bonding. Gas-phase acidity trends can reverse compared to solution phase due to the absence of solvent Born-solvation energy (e.g., gas-phase alkyl amine basicity and alcohol acidity order).
notes_list.mechanism_steps: 1. Deprotonate the acidic site to form the conjugate anion ($A^-$). 2. Assess periodic table position: Across a row, higher electronegativity stabilizes charge ($C^- < N^- < O^- < F^-$); down a group, larger atomic radius accommodates negative charge better ($F^- < Cl^- < Br^- < I^-$). 3. Evaluate resonance: Count equivalent canonical forms delocalizing negative charge onto electronegative atoms. 4. Check hybridization of the anionic atom: $sp$ (50% s-character) > $sp^2$ (33%) > $sp^3$ (25%). 5. Apply inductive effects: $-I$ groups near the charge disperse electron density and increase acidity ($d$-block distance dependence: $\alpha > \beta > \gamma$). 6. Check for special effects: Aromatic conjugate base formation or Ortho-effect in aromatic acids.
notes_list.kinetics_and_energy: $pKa = -\log_{10} K_a$, where $K_a$ is the acid dissociation equilibrium constant. $\Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K_a = 2.303 RT (pKa)$. A decrease of 1 unit in $pKa$ corresponds to a 10-fold increase in acidity ($\sim 1.36 \text{ kcal/mol}$ lowering of conjugate base free energy at 298 K).
notes_list.selectivity_and_stereochemistry: Enables quantitative prediction of relative $pKa$ rankings in substituted phenols, benzoic acids, dicarboxylic acids (e.g., Maleic vs Fumaric acid $pKa_1$ and $pKa_2$ differences due to intramolecular H-bonding), active methylene compounds (e.g., Acetylacetone $pKa = 9$ vs Diethyl malonate $pKa = 13$), and tautomeric equilibria.
notes_list.common_traps: 1. Confounding $+M$ and $-I$ for halogens: Fluorine has the strongest $-I$ effect, making $\alpha$-fluoro acids stronger than $\alpha$-chloro acids, but ortho-halophenols follow complex intramolecular H-bonding patterns. 2. Confusing acidity with rate of reaction: Acidity is a thermodynamic equilibrium property ($K_a$), not a kinetic rate ($k$). 3. Ignoring distance in inductive effects: $-I$ effect diminishes rapidly beyond 3 carbon bonds.
